headlines.article_text: McDonald's (MCD) Q3 2026 earnings Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points McDonald's quarterly earnings topped expectations, but its revenue fell short of estimates. The chain's U.S. same-store sales declined, but CEO Chris Kempczinski said its domestic performance is improving. McDonald's has leaned into discounts to attract budget-conscious diners over the last two years. In this article MCD Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT McDonald's logo sign is seen in Berlin, Germany, on September 12, 2026. Marcin Golba | Nurphoto | Getty Images McDonald's on Wednesday reported mixed quarterly results as traffic to its U.S. restaurants fell, leading to a slight decline in domestic same-store sales. The fast-food giant reported a 0.2% decrease in sales at its U.S. restaurants that have been open at least 13 months. Even so, the segment performed better than the 0.5% decline that Wall Street anticipated, according to a survey of analysts by StreetAccount. "In the U.S., we're encouraged by improvement as the quarter progressed following our intervention on value," McDonald's CEO Chris Kempczinski said in a statement. McDonald's same-store sales returned to growth in September after falling in July and August, CFO Ian Borden said on the company's earnings conference call. However, in response to an analyst question, he clarified that he did not say that U.S. same-store sales would be better in the fourth quarter. Kempczinski said in August that the company's U.S. business was falling short on execution, particularly on the implementation of its value offerings. Like many restaurants, McDonald's has leaned into discounts to attract budget-conscious diners over the last two years. To reverse same-store sales declines, McDonald's focused its marketing on its Extra Value Meals and restarted regional and national promotions on its mobile app, which are important to its most frequent diners. As McDonald's tries to regain its footing in the U.S., the chain is also testing two new value menus, one with mix and match bundles and the other with set combinations of menu items, executives said on the earnings call. The offering that resonates the most with customers and franchisees will be rolled out across the U.S. in early 2027. Shares of the company rose about 6% in afternoon trading. Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $3.57 adjusted vs. $3.38 expected Revenue: $7.16 billion vs. $7.29 billion expected The company reported third-quarter net income of $2.49 billion, or $3.51 per share, up from $2.28 billion, or $3.18 per share, a year earlier. Excluding restructuring charges and other items, McDonald's earned $3.57 per share. Net revenue rose 1% to $7.16 billion. The company's same-store sales rose 1.5%, lifted by its international segments. That topped analysts' expectations of a 1.3% increase, according to StreetAccount. McDonald's international developmental licensed markets business, which includes Japan and China, reported same-store sales growth of 4.2%. Wall Street was forecasting same-store sales to rise 2.1% for the division, based on StreetAccount estimates. The company's international operated division, which includes top markets like Australia and Germany, saw same-store sales growth of 1.4%. Still, the business underperformed Wall Street's expectations. Analysts were projecting same-store sales would rise 2.1%, according to StreetAccount. "In the majority of our large international markets, we're holding or gaining share," Borden said on the company's conference call. "It's a soft consumer environment, but we're doing well." France was a weak spot, McDonald's said. Kempczinski said that franchisees in France recently voted on a strategy to turn the business around. In addition to a softer economy in the country, McDonald's has also seen short-term disruptions related to student protests. headlines.article_text: Apple and other big tech stocks surge after 2026 midterm elections Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Many of the biggest technology companies are surging on Wednesday, after Democrats scored a seismic victory in the midterm elections, flipping both the House and Senate. Tuesday's election results remove uncertainty in the market, David Kelly, chief global strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management, said on "Squawk on the Street." Many of the technology stocks rising on Wednesday are what are known as hyperscalers, and analysts say they are poised to benefit from increased regulation. In this article GOOGL MSFT META AMZN AAPL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Apple's new CEO John Ternus holds the new iPhone 18 as he attends iPhone launch day at the Apple Fifth Avenue store in New York City on September 18, 2026, for the debut of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. Timothy A. Clary | Afp | Getty Images Many of the biggest technology companies are surging on Wednesday, after Democrats scored a seismic victory in the midterm elections, flipping both the House and Senate. During trading on Wednesday, Amazon surged 8%, Google rose over 6%, Microsoft rose 4%, Meta was up 3%, and Apple — which faced Trump's tariffs and recently got refunds — climbed nearly 7%. Tuesday's results remove uncertainty in the market, David Kelly, chief global strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management, said on "Squawk on the Street." He said the divided government would lead to "moderation in growth, moderation in inflation, less uncertainty, and I think that's all helping the stock market move up today." However, some stocks, particularly those tied to Trump advisor Elon Musk as well as the AI data center buildout, fell on Wednesday. As results came in last night, some observers saw bad news for big technology companies because of their bets to build large AI-focused data centers. There were 41 local ballot measures on Tuesday to place restrictions or clear the way for AI data centers, and voters sided against data centers in 40 of them. In a CNBC Voter Poll, 56% of voters said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their voting decision. Analysts said that Democrats who proposed data center moratoriums won gubernatorial races in Texas, Georgia, and Ohio, raising fears that projects could get snarled in regulation or blocked by politicians. "Recall that backup power emissions, zoning, water, interconnect/grid, and tax considerations are often overseen by state regulators," Macquarie analyst Paul Golding said in a note on Wednesday. Tesla stock fell 2%, and SpaceX was down 3%. Nvidia, which makes the chips for most of these AI data center projects, slipped just over 1%. Many of the technology stocks rising on Wednesday are what are known as hyperscalers, or the largest cloud providers that also pair massive capex spending with robust free cash flow and have the most experience and capability to construct AI data centers. "We believe higher regulatory barriers entrench incumbents, and increase risks (and raise required ROICs) for new entrants," wrote Needham analyst Laura Martin in a note on Wednesday. "Hyperscalers are AI incumbents." Smaller AI cloud providers, often called neoclouds, got whacked on Wednesday. CoreWeave stock fell 10%. Baird analysts said in a note that the election results create a "sentiment headwind" for neoclouds. Golding, the Macquarie analyst, wrote that he remains bullish on AI infrastructure, and that well-capitalized, high-quality operators stand to benefit the most if projects in some states slow down. "Neoclouds may pay more to lease powered shells for GPUaaS commitments (and pass on costs), while hyperscaler/AI lab capacity needs could intensify competition for even more limited supply," Golding wrote. Tuesday's results could signal restrictions on new data center developments in some states, but it doesn't necessarily signal a nationwide slowdown in construction, Chris Miglino, CEO of Axe Compute , said in an email. Companies are still raising capital, enterprises are spending, and there's still a need for more capacity. Miglino said that increased regulation in some regions could cause investors and customers to look more closely at different cloud computing providers, and opt for those with the capability to deliver capacity, or which offer AI inference to a specific industry niche. "If you've already secured power, have the financing in place and understand how to deploy and operate compute infrastructure efficiently, you're in a much stronger position than a company that's still trying to figure those things out," Miglino said. headlines.title: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: CoreWeave, Micron, Booking Holdings, McDonald's, CVS Health & more
headlines.summary: Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading.
headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: CRWV, MU, BKNG, MCD, CVS Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading. AI infrastructure — Companies tied to data centers slid following Democrats' midterm election victories as traders prepared for a slowdown in the buildout effort . The iShares A.I. Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) slid more than 2%. Shares of Comfort Systems and Vistra tumbled 17% and 13%, respectively. Memory stocks Micron and Sandisk lost 5% and 7%. Defense stocks — Shares of defense companies tumbled after Democrats swept Congress in the midterm elections. The iShares U.S. Aerospace & Defense ETF (ITA) slipped more than 1%; Lockheed Martin 's stock fell 6%. Shares of Howmet Aerospace and Northrop Grumman lost more than 4%. Trump Media & Technology Group — Shares of President Donald Trump 's social media and tech company were down 11% after a decisive victory by Democrats in the midterms Tuesday night. Trump owns 41% of the company, which owns social media platform Truth Social. Democrats taking control of Congress add a check on the president's policies. Tesla , SpaceX — Shares of Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX dropped 3% each. The moves come after the Democrats won control of the House of Representatives and the Senate. Many of the newly elected candidates have criticized the rapid data center buildout that's been fueled by artificial intelligence. SpaceX operates an AI supercomputing infrastructure in Tennessee and Mississippi , while Tesla has one in Texas. Neocloud stocks — Shares of so-called neocloud companies moved lower, with CoreWeave 's stock dropping 9%, shares of Iren tumbling 11% and shares of Nebius slipping about 6%. The Democratic wins in Texas and rejection of data centers in ballots across the country are expected to create hurdles for data center plays. Trimble — The software company's stock tanked almost 18%. Trimble said it anticipates organic annual recurring revenue growth of roughly 10% for 2026, down from its previous call for a range of 12% to 14%. Fidelity National Information Services — The financial software stock tumbled 24% after the company slashed its full-year earnings outlook. FIS sees adjusted earnings per share in a range of $5.82 to $5.89. That's down from a prior forecast of $6.15 per share to $6.24 per share. AppLovin — Shares rallied more than 10% as traders awaited the company's third-quarter results after the bell Wednesday. Analysts polled by FactSet expected AppLovin to report earnings per share of $4.03 on revenue of $2.075 billion. Clear Secure — Shares soared 33% after the identity verification company lifted its forecast for free cash flow for the full year. Clear Secure sees at least $490 million in free cash flow, topping the FactSet consensus estimate of $482.9 million. Third-quarter results also topped the Street's estimates. Consumer discretionary stocks — Cyclical stocks that sell to consumers rallied after better-than-expected results from Booking Holdings . Shares of Booking and Expedia jumped 11% and 13%, respectively. Nike 's stock rallied more than 6%, and shares of Amazon climbed almost 7%. Novo Nordisk — Shares gained over 6% after the global healthcare company reported earnings of 5.79 Danish kroner, or about 63 cents per share, compared with Wall Street expectations of 5.10 kroner, or about 55 cents. The company raised its fiscal 2026 outlook, citing expectations for GLP-1 product sales. McDonald's — The fast-food restaurant chain reported mixed quarterly results , sending shares 5% higher. Adjusted earnings came in at $3.57 per share, topping the $3.38 expected from analysts polled by LSEG. However, its revenue of $7.16 billion fell short of the $7.29 billion consensus estimate. CVS Health — Shares fell more than 12% after the company said it would split into two separate publicly traded companies by the first half of 2028. The move would reverse CVS' $78 billion acquisition of Aetna and separate the company's retail pharmacy business. Duolingo — Shares surged 32% after the language learning software company reported third-quarter revenue of $309 million. That topped an LSEG consensus of $303 million. Monthly active users totaled 153 million for the quarter, exceeding a 149 million forecast. Adjusted EBITDA margin also topped expectations. Block — The fintech stock rallied almost 16% after Block posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that exceeded expectations, and raised guidance for the full year ending December. Adjusted earnings of $1.13 per share topped the $1.03 LSEG consensus estimate, while revenue of $6.72 billion beat the $6.59 billion consensus. Renewable energy stocks — Shares of renewable energy companies moved higher after the Democratic sweep of Congress. Shares of Sunrun and Plug Power each climbed roughly 7%, while shares of Nextpower jumped 15%. Datadog — The cloud monitoring company saw shares sink 14% after it released its third-quarter financial results. While it beat on both the top and bottom lines, its revenue guidance came in soft. Datadog expects revenue of $1.19 billion to $1.20 billion for the fourth quarter, versus the $1.20 billion consensus estimate. Kraft Heinz — The food and beverage manufacturer's stock gained 6%. Kraft Heinz said it will divest its North America coffee business to One Rock Capital Partners. The company also reported adjusted earnings of 53 cents per share on revenue of $6.12 billion for its third quarter, topping expectations. Analysts polled by LSEG had expected EPS of 42 cents on revenue of $6.09 billion. — CNBC's Darla Mercado, Deena Zaidi, Paulina Likos, Sarah Min, Davis Giangiulio, Ananya Chetia, Fred Imbert, Scott Schnipper and Nick Wells contributed reporting.

Aaron Schwartz | Getty Images President Donald Trump turned against Fox News on Tuesday night in a string of posts on Truth Social while Democratic wins rolled in during a historic midterm election. Trump blamed the network, which he's long championed, for Republican losses, saying in one post on his social media network that it "bears responsibility for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition." Democrats took control of both the Senate and House of Representatives, flipping seats in states usually favorable to Republicans, including Texas, South Carolina and Kansas. Trump also pointed to Fox's recent ratings as evidence of the network's decline. "FoxNews Ratings are way down (27%!) because they're spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats! All of those people who used to watch Fox, and no longer do, get it. It's them, not me," he posted. Fox News did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In a press release last week, Fox News reported 1.1 million average viewers for October, down about 27% from the same month a year prior. Fox Corp. CEO Lachlan Murdoch noted the decline during the company's quarterly earnings call on Monday, citing "viewer fatigue." However, Murdoch said such a shift is expected in the lead-up to a midterm election with a second-term president and said it was not the result of viewers turning to competitors' coverage. "Those viewers are not going to any other news channel. They're not switching to MS NOW or to CNN," he said. "They're just fatigued and watching slightly less television overall." Versant -owned MS NOW and Skydance -owned CNN both reported primetime viewership was up by double digits in October compared with the year-ago period. However, both networks still had smaller total-day average audiences than Fox News. MS NOW had 588,000 average viewers in October across all day parts, and CNN had 402,000, according to Nielsen data cited by Fox. Despite Fox News' year-over-year drop in viewership, the company reported an otherwise strong quarter in what Murdoch called an "outstanding start to fiscal 2027." Fox Corp., which includes the linear TV networks as well as entertainment and sports assets and a streaming business, reported revenue for its fiscal first quarter of $4.57 billion, up 22% year over year. The company pointed to strength in advertising revenue, which increased 47%, buoyed by strong political advertising and the FIFA Men's World Cup, which aired in part on Fox platforms across June and July. While he's repeatedly taken aim at NBC and Disney -owned ABC, the president has had a much friendlier relationship with Fox and its networks. The plan would specifically separate CVS' roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation's three largest PBMs. The decision follows a "comprehensive strategic review" by the company's board of directors, according to a news release . Shares of CVS fell more than 12% on Wednesday. It's a stunning reversal for the healthcare powerhouse, which has spent the last two decades working to turn itself into a one-stop health destination. The move also comes as CVS' aggressive turnaround plan under CEO David Joyner shows substantial progress, with the company pursuing $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shake-ups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs. But Joyner told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " on Wednesday that the decision to split is "out of a position of strength," pointing to recovery in Aetna's Medicare business and solid performance in the retail pharmacy. "So it's all about the strength of the business that affords us the opportunity to make what we think are the right strategic decisions for the future of this company," he later added. A person walks into a CVS pharmacy near George Washington University in Washington, U.S., August 15, 2024. Kaylee Greenlee Beal | Reuters CVS shares have jumped roughly 70% since Joyner took the helm in October 2024, bringing the company's market value to $117 billion. The two new companies would both be publicly traded. The insurance and PBM company will retain the CVS Health name and be run by Joyner, while the other company will be called CVS Pharmacy and be led by Prem Shah, who is currently group president of CVS Health. Additional leadership positions and board members will be announced at a later date, CVS said. Existing CVS shareholders will own stock in both companies after the split. The Financial Times on Tuesday first reported the breakup plans. The company's pharmacy business raked in $37.66 billion in 2025 sales, while its insurance unit booked $36.29 billion in revenue and the healthcare services segment generated $51.24 billion. CVS on Wednesday also posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that topped Wall Street expectations. Total sales climbed to $108.40 billion, from $102.87 billion in the prior-year period. Sales were boosted by year-over-year growth in the company's healthcare benefits and health services segments. Meanwhile, revenue in its pharmacy services business slid from the previous year. How the CVS split would work On Wednesday, CVS said it will lump its insurer and PBM with its primary care business Oak Street Health, home visit provider Signify Health and the company's specialty drug business. CVS also said the split will allow the two companies to experience a "focused strategic agenda" and greater ability to "innovate, adopt technology, increase efficiency," among other benefits. It's not the first time CVS has weighed splitting the company. In October 2024, CVS engaged advisors in a strategic review of its business and considered breaking up its retail pharmacy and insurance units. But Joyner told CNBC that the company was "in a turnaround" at that time without the flexibility, cash position or business performance to execute a split. In an interview, Leerink Partners analyst Michael Cherny said the split shows "the stability of the pharmacy," which has won market share from competitors and is seeing gross margins stabilize thanks to CostVantage, a new pharmacy reimbursement model introduced by CVS last year that the company bills as more transparent. "This business is a much different business from the one that's been considered three years ago, five years ago, 10 years ago, where there had been a litany of headwinds that the pharmacy just couldn't overcome," he told CNBC on Wednesday. One potential concern for investors is whether the retail pharmacy will lose its competitive advantage of being directly linked with a PBM, which negotiates drug prices and manages prescription drug benefits on behalf of insurers and employers. But Joyner told analysts Wednesday that the synergy between the two businesses "are going to be preserved in commercial agreements between the two organizations," adding that "we don't need the integration of an operating structure." Cherny said the rationale for the split could also extend to the state legislative scrutiny over the company's level of vertical integration. The potential breakup also comes as pharmacy benefit managers face mounting bipartisan scrutiny in Washington, D.C., and across states. Republicans in Tennessee and Arkansas have passed laws that would ban co-ownership of PBMs and pharmacies. Those have been challenged in court by CVS and other companies. PBMs have been criticized for opaque pricing practices, their growing market power and potential conflicts of interest when they are owned by companies that also operate insurers and pharmacies.
